hints_cache: This is a greedy construction problem. To get the lexicographically smallest string, we should try to assign 'a' to as many positions as possible, then 'b', and so on, up to 'z'.

Focus on the requirement that if lcp[i][j] > 0, then the characters at index i and index j must be identical. You can iterate through the indices and 'group' them under the same character if the matrix says they match.

Once you've built a candidate string, you can't just trust it! The greedy step only ensures characters match where the matrix says they should, but it doesn't guarantee they *don't* match where the matrix says they shouldn't.

To verify your string, you need to reconstruct the LCP matrix from your candidate string using dynamic programming. The core logic is: if word[i] == word[j], then their LCP is 1 plus the LCP of the suffixes starting at i+1 and j+1.
Finally, compare your reconstructed matrix with the input. If they match perfectly, and you didn't need more than 26 letters, you've found your answer; otherwise, no such string exists.
